learn.title: What a leak is
learn.body: A memory leak is heap memory you allocated and never freed, and can no longer reach. The program keeps running, so nothing looks wrong. But the memory stays reserved until the program ends. A long-running app that leaks a little each time can eventually run out.

learn.title: A leaky loop
learn.body: This prints 0, 1, 2. Each pass asks for 100 ints, which is 400 bytes, and then loses the pointer when `p` goes out of scope. Three passes leak 1200 bytes. Adding `free(p);` at the end of the loop fixes it.

learn.title: Finding leaks with Valgrind
learn.body: Valgrind is a tool, common on Linux, that runs your program and reports memory mistakes. Compile with `-g` so it can show line numbers, then run the program under it. It lists blocks that were allocated but never freed. It is not available on every system.

learn.title: Running it
learn.body: Valgrind prints a summary of leaked bytes and where each block was allocated. A clean run ends with a message saying that all heap blocks were freed.

learn.title: Reading a report
learn.body: Imagine Valgrind says some bytes are definitely lost, with a `malloc` line from your loop.
steps: The report points at the line that allocated the block
Find where that pointer is last used
Add `free` there, before the pointer is lost

learn.body: A leak rarely crashes anything. Only a tool or careful reading shows it, so check with Valgrind whenever you use `malloc`.

questions.prompt: Does a leak usually stop the program at once?
questions.explanation: Leaks are quiet, which is why you need tools to find them.
